HIV-1 isolates from 2 out of 39 patients receiving combination therapy with didanosine and zidovudine for up to 2 years showed decreased susceptibility to didanosine, lamivudine, stavudine, zalcitabine, and zidovudine in cell culture. 4. Data from clinical studies indicate that the presence of thymidine analogue mutations (M41L, D67N, L210W, T215Y, K219Q) reduces the response to didanosine. 6. Lifetime carcinogenicity studies were conducted in mice and rats for 22 and 24 months, respectively. 7. Didanosine did not cause a significant increase in neoplastic lesions in mice or rats at maximally tolerated doses. 13. Didanosine was positive in the following genetic toxicology assays: The Escherichia coli WP2 uvrA bacterial mutagenicity assay. The L5178Y/TK+/mouse lymphoma mammalian cell gene mutation assay. The in vitro chromosomal aberration assay in cultured human peripheral lymphocytes. The in vitro chromosomal aberration assay in Chinese hamster lung cells. The BALB/c 3T3 in vitro transformation assay. 14. No evidence of mutagenicity was observed in an Ames Salmonella bacterial mutagenicity assay or in rat and mouse in vivo micronucleus assays. 15. Evidence of dose-limiting skeletal muscle toxicity was observed in mice and rats (but not in dogs) following long-term dosing (greater than 90 days) with didanosine at doses approximately 1. 16. The relationship of this finding to the potential for didanosine to cause myopathy in humans is unclear. However, human myopathy has been associated with the administration of didanosine and other nucleoside analogues. 17. Study AI454-152 was a 48-week, randomized, open-label study comparing didanosine delayed-release capsules (400 mg once daily) plus stavudine (40 mg twice daily) plus nelfinavir (750 mg three times daily) to zidovudine (300 mg) plus lamivudine (150 mg) combination tablets twice daily plus nelfinavir (750 mg three times daily) in 511 treatment-naive patients. 18. The mean CD4 cell count at baseline was 411 cells/mm³ (range: 39 to 1105 cells/mm³), and the mean plasma HIV-1 RNA was 4.71 log10 copies/mL (range: 2.8 to 5.9 log10 copies/mL). 19. Patients were primarily male (72%) and Caucasian (53%), with a mean age of 35 years (range: 18 to 73 years). 20. The percentages of patients with HIV-1 RNA less than 400 and less than 50 copies/mL and outcomes through 48 weeks are summarized in Figure 1 and Table 13, respectively. 21. Efficacy in pediatric patients was demonstrated in a randomized, double-blind, controlled study (ACTG 152, conducted 1991–1995) involving 831 patients aged 3 months to 18 years treated for more than 1.5 years with zidovudine (180 mg/m² every 6 hours), didanosine (120 mg/m² every 12 hours), or zidovudine (120 mg/m² every 6 hours) plus didanosine (90 mg/m² every 12 hours). 22. Patients treated with didanosine or didanosine plus zidovudine had lower rates of HIV-1 disease progression or death compared to those treated with zidovudine alone. 23. Didanosine delayed-release capsules are available in bottles of 30 capsules in the following strengths: 200 mg, 250 mg, and 400 mg. 24. Store didanosine at 20°C to 25°C (68°F to 77°F). 25. Patients should be informed that pancreatitis, a serious and potentially fatal toxicity, may occur with didanosine, whether used alone or in combination regimens. 26. Patients should be advised that peripheral neuropathy, characterized by numbness, tingling, or pain in the hands or feet, may develop during therapy with didanosine delayed-release capsules. 27. Peripheral neuropathy occurs most frequently in patients with advanced HIV-1 disease or a history of peripheral neuropathy, and discontinuation of didanosine may be required if toxicity develops. 28. Patients should be informed that lactic acidosis and severe hepatomegaly with steatosis, including fatal cases, have been reported with nucleoside analogues, including didanosine. 29. Hepatotoxicity, including fatal hepatic adverse events, has been reported in patients with preexisting liver dysfunction. 30. The safety and efficacy of didanosine delayed-release capsules have not been established in HIV-infected patients with significant underlying liver disease. 31. Non-cirrhotic portal hypertension has been reported in patients taking didanosine, including cases leading to liver transplantation or death. 32. Retinal changes and optic neuritis have been reported in both adult and pediatric patients. 33. Redistribution or accumulation of body fat may occur in patients receiving antiretroviral therapy, and the cause and long-term health effects of these conditions are not yet known. 34. When didanosine is used in combination with other agents with similar toxicities, the incidence of adverse events may be higher than when didanosine is used alone. 35. Patients should be closely monitored. 36. Patients should be cautioned about using medications or substances, including alcohol, that may exacerbate didanosine toxicities. 37. Didanosine delayed-release capsules are not a cure for HIV-1 infection, and patients may continue to experience illnesses associated with HIV-1, including opportunistic infections. 38. Patients should remain under the care of a physician while using didanosine. 39. Patients should be advised to avoid behaviors that can spread HIV-1 to others, such as sharing needles or personal items that may have blood or body fluids on them, and engaging in unprotected sex. 40. Safe sex practices, including the use of latex or polyurethane condoms or other barrier methods, should be followed to reduce the risk of sexual transmission of HIV-1. 41. Patients should not breastfeed, as HIV-1 can be transmitted to the baby through breast milk, and it is unknown if didanosine is excreted in breast milk or if it could harm the baby. 42. Patients should be instructed to swallow the capsule whole and not open it.
